newsitem.title: USA: Festive Continental hands out bonus checks.
newsitem.headline: Festive Continental hands out bonus checks.

text.p: While a Dixieland band played "We're in the Money," Continental Airlines Chairman Gordon Bethune handed out profit-sharing checks to employees on Friday and got in a few digs at troubled Texas-based rival American Airlines.

Bethune said he hoped American, embroiled in eleventh-hour contract negotiations with its pilots, could avoid a strike but that his airline was gearing up to pick up the slack should Fort Worth-based American, a unit of AMR Corp. , be forced to shut down.

"Isn't great to work for a winner? Go over a couple of terminals and see the difference between (American) and an airline that works as a team," Bethune told employees in a festive ceremony at Houston Intercontinental Airport, Continental's main hub.
"We're out passing out checks and they're out there on the picket line," he said. "That used to be us. Now we're on top and every dog's got its day."

Bethune rolled up to the ceremony in an armoured Brink's truck where he was greeted by uproarious applause from Continental workers awaiting their $68 million in profit-sharing checks. He smiled broadly when a Brink's guard walked on stage with a large sack marked with a dollar sign.

Continental, which has twice emerged from bankruptcy but posted record profits in 1996, began the payouts last year to reward employees for helping the company achieve financial objectives. The first payout was about 3.5 percent of each employee's salary, but this year it was 7 percent.

After handing out checks, Bethune told reporters that Continental would add employees and extra flights to handle an expected increase in traffic if American's contract talks fail and its pilots go out on strike Friday night as threatened.

"We hope it doesn't happen ... (but) we put on some extra sections (flights) ... only because we believe there might be a bunch of stranded people. If there is, we want to take them if we can," he said.
"American represents about 20 percent of our industry seats, so the pie's going to go up that much," Bethune said.
He expressed confidence that Continental, whose own pilots have said they will seek a pay raise when contract negotiations begin in April, could avoid American's current predicament.

"We've gone through the flight attendants, dispatchers and other employee groups and you haven't heard a ripple. I would expect we'll come to something fair with our pilots and get on with it," he said.

Bethune said that Continental, which faced wrenching labour problems during its bankruptcy proceedings, had learned from the experience. He said a strike at American, based just 250 miles to the north, would allow everyone to see firsthand the devastating effects of a labour stoppage.
"You all win together or you lose together -- there can't be winners or losers on the same team. We're not going to let that happen here at Continental ever again," he said.
